title: Unplugging
hook: many put away phones and screens for the day
tomorrow: walk slowly on Shabbat, or run? two teachings disagree.

segments.voice: Yesterday, zemirot: a hum at the table, and the meal doesn't want to end. Sing at the table. Today, what goes quiet so the singing can be heard.

Sunday morning, the phone posts its weekly screen-time report, and the number is rarely smaller than hoped. Now a puzzle. The Torah says don't work on the Sabbath. It never mentions phones, screens, or anything with a battery. So why do some Jews put their phones in a drawer from Friday sunset until Saturday night? The answer starts somewhere strange: in the middle of a set of building instructions.
screen: `THE WEEKLY SCREEN-TIME REPORT.` → `THE TORAH NEVER SAYS PHONE.` → `SO WHY THE DRAWER?`

segments.voice: Exodus spends chapters on the Mishkan, the portable sanctuary in the desert: boards, curtains, gold, oil. And right in the middle of the instructions, it stops to say: keep the Sabbath. Then the building resumes. The rabbis read that placement as a clue. The kinds of work it took to build the sanctuary are the work you rest from on the seventh day. The Hebrew word is melakhah. The Mishnah lists its kinds, forty less one: sowing, kneading, weaving, writing, building, lighting a fire, carrying from one domain to another. Notice what the list is about. Not sweat. Making, shaping, changing the world. Six days a week people do that, the way God does in Genesis. On the seventh they stop, the way God does. And the commandment hands the day off to the whole household: children, workers, the stranger, even the animals. Nobody in the house is on call. Now the phone. In Orthodox practice, switching devices on and off counts as forbidden work, so the phone stays off. Jews who don't keep that law sometimes unplug anyway, by choice, because a phone is a pocket-size workshop: buying, posting, replying, fixing. One to tell a friend tonight: Abraham Joshua Heschel called the Sabbath a palace in time, a building you enter by stopping. Puzzle solved. The Torah didn't have to name the phone. It named what the phone does.
screen: `KEEP THE SABBATH, MID-BLUEPRINT.` · `MELAKHAH: THE WORK OF MAKING.` · `A PHONE IS A POCKET WORKSHOP.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · then, large: `UNPLUGGED.`

segments.voice: Choose your hours: a stretch of this coming Shabbat, or of any day this week, when the phone goes in a drawer, screen down, out of reach. Decide now where it will sit, and who should know you'll be off. Then let your hands rest empty in your lap and notice what they want to reach for.
Unplugging: resting from melakhah, the work of making and changing the world, so the phone goes quiet too.
For today: unplugged, not punished, just off duty from changing the world for a day. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1668 COUNTS.` → `SHABBAT, LIVED · 6 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: WALK SLOWLY ON SHABBAT, OR RUN?`

howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat by traditional law leave phones and screens off from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall; others choose a phone-free stretch of the day as rest, often keeping the device in a drawer or another room.

notes: Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 says 'forty less one'; the voice keeps that phrasing and lists a few examples. Confirm the examples (sowing, kneading, weaving, writing, building, kindling, carrying between domains) are on the list.
Shabbat 49b: the categories correspond to the labors of the Mishkan (learned from the juxtaposition in Exodus 35); paraphrased. Confirm.

Orthodox practice on devices described simply ('switching devices on and off counts as forbidden work'); the reasons vary among authorities (building, kindling, completing). Confirm the plain wording is fair, and that 'Jews who don't keep that law sometimes unplug by choice' reads without ranking.
Heschel's 'palace in time' is paraphrased from The Sabbath (in copyright); not quoted.
Outline hook says 'many put away phones'; the voice says 'some Jews' to keep to the claims rule.
